A new report from the AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety reveals that hit-and-run car crash deaths are on the rise, and almost 70 percent of the victims are pedestrians or those riding bicycles. The increase in deaths is partly caused by an increase in people riding their bicycles to work or as a form of exercise. If you were injured or lost a loved one in a bicycle accident, our Charleston personal injury lawyers may be able to help you pursue compensation. We offer a free, no obligation legal consultation and do not charge for representing you unless you receive fair compensation.

Reducing the Risk of a Bicycle Crash

Fortunately, there are many ways that cyclists can reduce the risk of being injured in a bicycle crash, including:

Being Careful at Intersections

Intersections are some of the most dangerous locations for cyclists, which is why you need to be extremely careful when approaching these areas and riding through them. Slow down when approaching an intersection and look carefully for approaching traffic. Even if you have the right of way, check that no other vehicles are coming. Carefully monitor traffic signs and signals – if a light is about to change, you might be better waiting to go through the intersection.  As you go through the intersection, watch for any approaching cars. You want as much time as possible to maneuver to avoid a collision if a car is coming at you.

Increasing Visibility

Bicyclists take up less space and are less noticeable than other vehicles. For these reasons, it is important that cyclists take care to increase their visibility. There are several ways to accomplish this, including:
  • Wearing light-colored or luminescent clothing day and night when cycling
  • Adding reflective tape to clothing
  • Using a rear reflector on your bike
  • Avoiding blind spots
  • Avoiding emerging from a covered area without stopping or looking for dangers ahead
  • Avoiding riding on a narrow rural road when it is dark outside

Signaling Properly

Signaling properly allows other motorists to know your intentions. The following signals should be used:
  • Left-hand turn – Signal by extending your left arm to the side and keeping it level with the left side of your bike.
  • Right-hand turn – Extend your right arm and hand, keeping it level with the rest of your body.

Avoiding Parked Cars

Many drivers do not look for approaching bike riders before opening their car doors after parking. This often results in bicyclists crashing into open car doors, particularly when cars are parallel parked. You can reduce your risk of this type of accident by putting at least four feet between your bike and any parked cars. You should also check parked cars for drivers or passengers so you will be prepared in case one of them opens a door. The more time you have to react, the more likely you are to avoid an accident.

Wearing a Helmet

While wearing a helmet will not prevent an accident from happening, it can help minimize any damage an accident causes and potentially save your life. Some guidelines for bike helmets include:
  • The helmet and straps should fit snugly on your head.
  • The helmet should be level.
  • Use a brightly-colored helmet with reflective tape to increase visibility.

Contact a Lawyer for Assistance

Sometimes no matter how safe you are, others may cause you to suffer injury in a bicycle accident. Contacting an experienced personal injury lawyer can help you protect your claim. At Roden Law, our team of legal professionals can help you seek compensation for the many costs involved in an accident, such as medical expenses, lost wages, and other damages. If you were injured in a bike accident, we can explain your rights during a free initial consultation. Since we only collect attorney’s fees if we help you recover compensation, you have nothing to lose by scheduling a free, no-obligation consultation to discuss your rights.

Although many auto collisions are attributed to driver negligence, poor road conditions are also a common contributing factor to many car accidents. When this occurs, there may be several parties at fault for your accident, including local, state and federal government agencies. The Charleston auto accident attorneys at Roden Law have handled numerous car accident claims and know how to identify which parties can be held liable for the damages you suffered. Contact us to schedule a free, no obligation consultation as soon as possible after an accident. We will review your claim to determine if you may be entitled to compensation for your medical expenses, lost wages and pain and suffering. Below, our Charleston personal injury lawyers review several factors that may help us determine which party is liable for a car accident caused by hazardous roadway conditions.

Common Roadway Hazards

In Georgia, there are several types of dangerous conditions that create hazard for drivers. Although some hazards may seem common, they still increase the likelihood of causing a serious car accident. These roadway hazards may include:

Potholes

When a vehicle runs into a pothole, it can cause serious damage to a vehicle and may even result in an accident. Potholes are the result of expanding and contracting groundwater below the pavement. As this occurs, the roadway will start to give way, and the size of the pothole will continue to increase as cars run over it if not fixed.

Poor Roadway Maintenance

Failing to properly maintain roadways can lead to several hazards that increase the risk of an auto accident, including:
  • Uneven pavement
  • Erosion
  • Faded lane markings
  • Broken guardrails
  • Missing traffic signs

Dangerous Roadway Design

Even with proper construction, poor design of a roadway can put motorists in danger. Flaws in roadway design can cause dangerous conditions that increase the risk of an accident, such as:
  • Curves that are too sharp
  • Merging lanes or on-ramps that are too short
  • Poor lighting
  • Inadequate warnings of dangerous conditions

Who is Responsible for Maintaining the Roadway?

In Georgia, cities, counties and state government agencies are responsible for maintaining roadways and ensuring any known hazard is fixed. There are several factors that may determine which entity is responsible for fixing the hazard, such as the location of the roadway and type of hazard. However, there may be instances where multiple agencies are liable for the same roadway. For example, the state may be responsible for filling a pothole while the county or city is responsible for clearing the roadway of debris. When a hazardous condition causes an accident, you must prove the responsible government entity neglected to maintain the roadway. This requires you to prove the at-fault entity failed to uphold its obligation to clear any known hazard, or adequately warn motorists of its existence. Additionally, if a dangerous roadway hazard long enough for the liable entity to know of its existence, but failed to become aware of the hazard, the government entity may still be held liable for any resulting damages.

Can I Sue a Government Agency in Georgia?

If you are injured in an auto accident that resulted from a government entity’s negligence, you may be able to file a personal injury claim against the at-fault entity. However, filing a personal injury claim against a government entity in Georgia is very different than bringing legal action against a person or corporation. This includes providing a written claim to the government entity responsible for causing the accident. Your claim should include the:
  • Time and place of the accident
  • Extent of your injury
  • Amount of damages you intend to pursue
  • Negligent action that caused your injury
Additionally, Georgia imposes a different time line for accident victims who are filing a personal injury claim against the government. If you are filing a claim against a city or municipal county, you have six months to provide notice about your claim. Likewise, if you are filing a claim against the state, you must present notice of your claim within 12 months of the accident. If you do not follow these strict deadlines, your claim will likely be dismissed and you cannot obtain compensation for your injury.

Contact an Attorney for Help

If you were injured in a car accident caused by poor road conditions, you may be entitled to compensation for your medical bills, lost wages, and pain and suffering. The Savannah car accident lawyers of Roden Law will evaluate your case and help you pursue the compensation you deserve. Schedule a free, no obligation consultation today and learn which legal options may be available for pursuing compensation for your injuries. We only work on a contingency fee basis, which means there are no upfront fees and you only have to pay us if we recover compensation for your claim.

There are about 13.2 million teen drivers on the road every day, according to data from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA). What happens when one of those teens is responsible for a motor vehicle accident resulting in injuries to you or a loved one? Call a Charleston car accident lawyer if you were involved in an accident with a teen driver to learn about your potential legal options. Below, we discuss some of the ways the teenage driver or his or her parent may be held liable for your damages.

Parental Liability

Almost every single state has parental liability laws in case their child causes death, injuries, property damage through negligent or willful acts that bring harm to others. Parents and any legal guardians who have custody of a minor may be held financially responsible for damages caused by the minor, including damages from a car accident. If a teen driver is responsible for the accident that caused your injuries, you may have legal recourse to pursue compensation from the teen’s parents. This usually means filing a claim against the parent or legal guardian’s car insurance policy. Teenagers usually cannot afford car insurance, which is why they are often on their parents’ plans. However, most insurance companies require that anyone residing in the same household who has a license is listed under the homeowner’s motor vehicle insurance policy. It is important to note that car insurance typically follows the car. Even if the teenager was not listed on the policy, if the car is owned and insured by the parent, the parent’s liability insurance likely applies.

What if the Teenager was Driving a Car Not Owned by His or Her Parents?

This could be a much more complicated situation. For example, maybe the teenager was driving a car loaned to the parents by someone else. If the teenager had permission to drive the car, the insurance on the car likely applies. However, if the teenager did not have permission, such as if the teenager’s parents told him or her not to drive the car, liability insurance on the car may not apply.

What About Willful or Malicious Actions?

It is important to note insurance policies often have exclusions for willful or malicious actions. If the teenager’s actions were intentional, insurance on the car may not apply. In these situations, it may be necessary to file a lawsuit.

Tips to Help Keep Your Own Teen Driver Safe

According to an NHTSA study, about 33 percent of high school students nationwide admitted to texting and driving while 12 percent of distracted drivers involved in fatal car accidents were teens aged 15 to 19. Statistics like these may have a sobering effect on parents who have children on the verge of getting a driver’s license. These statistics also highlight how important it is to discuss road safety with your teen as early as possible. There are also some practical things you can do to help keep your teen driver safe:
  • Talk to them about the dangers of distracted driving
  • Show them data about teen drivers in the U.S.
  • Lead by example and be a safe driver

Let Us Help. Call Today

Teen drivers cause thousands of accidents resulting in all sorts of injuries. If you or a loved one were injured due to a teenager’s negligent driving, you may be eligible to seek compensation from the liability insurance under the parent’s car insurance policy. Let our attorneys at Roden Law help you through this complicated process while you focus on recovering from your injuries. We have successfully recovered millions in compensation for injury victims since 2013. If you choose to hire us, the consultation is free, and you do not owe us anything unless we recover compensation on your behalf.

No matter the severity of an accident, if you plan on filing an insurance claim, you should contact law enforcement to investigate and file a police report. This report often serves as an important piece of evidence as your attorney works to validate your claim. Below, our Charleston car accident lawyers discuss the value of a police report in proving liability in an injury claim. We also explain how we may be able to help you through the claims process without any out-of-pocket costs to you.

Establishing an Objective Third-Party Narrative

When law enforcement officers arrive at an accident scene, their objective is not just to ensure the safety of those involved and the safe flow of traffic. They also need to complete a report that will serve as an objective third-party observation of what may have caused the crash. Police officers usually note several factors that may have contributed to an accident, including the following:
  • Weather conditions
  • Visibility conditions
  • Roadway conditions
  • Driver impairment
  • Speeding
The police report may also note how a driver may have acted negligently before an accident occurred and who may be to blame for the crash.

Witness Statements

When an accident only causes minor damage, injury victims may be able to collect witness information on their own while police conduct their investigation into the crash. But what happens when an accident results in serious injuries that render you or your passengers unconscious, which makes it impossible to collect witness statements? Fortunately, law enforcement officers can also collect witness statements and document them in the police report. Sometimes, passing drivers who witness an accident may call 9-1-1, but they do not stay at the scene. A police report may provide a statement from a passing driver, which you may not have been able to obtain on your own. For example, a passerby who witnesses a hit-and-run crash may call the police to report it. He or she may have a description of the vehicle and a license plate number. You may not have been able to obtain this information because of poor lighting, obstructions on the road or the fact you were seriously injured in the crash and rendered unconscious.

Traffic Citations

Police reports usually note which driver was issued a citation for a traffic violation, such as:
  • Speeding
  • Running a red light
  • Improperly passing
  • Following too closely
  • Texting and driving
  • And more
If the other driver involved in your accident gets a ticket, it may be a powerful piece of evidence to help prove liability.

Damage

The police report also describes damage to the vehicles involved in the accident. Sometimes this can help to prove liability for the crash. For example, liability is often clear in a two-vehicle accident in which one vehicle has damage to its front end while the other has damage only to its rear. The location of damage often indicates what drivers were doing before a crash occurred. Did they slow down? If there is severe damage to one vehicle, it may indicate the other driver was not paying attention. If one driver was not paying attention, he or she may have crashed into the other car without slowing down at all.

Injuries

One of the most common counterarguments made by an insurance company is that your injuries were not caused by the accident, but something else. They may say you are just looking for money for a preexisting injury. Having a police report that details your injuries and complaints at the scene may help prove that your injuries were, in fact, caused by the accident.

Schedule a Free Consultation. Call Us Today

Police reports are the result of a preliminary investigation and there are other pieces of evidence your lawyer may need to help prove liability for an accident claim. If the at-fault driver’s insurance company tries to deny liability, it is important to have an experienced attorney at your side to help validate your claim. At Roden Law, our attorneys have a proven track record of securing the compensation you need for medical bills, lost wages and other damages. There is no cost for our services unless we win your case.

If you are injured in an accident caused by someone else’s negligence, you may be eligible for compensation. However, the process of filing a claim and recovering the compensation you need for medical bills and other damages takes time. How do you pay for the medical treatment you need while your lawyer seeks a settlement? You can discuss your options for paying for medical care while your injury claim is being processed with a licensed car accident attorney in Charleston in a free consultation. We do not charge you anything up front and only get paid if you do.

File a Claim Through Your Own Car Insurance Policy

Unlike some other at-fault states, South Carolina does not offer Personal Injury Protection (PIP) coverage to drivers. PIP pays for the policyholder’s medical treatment. In South Carolina, drivers instead have the option to purchase Medical Payments (MedPay) coverage to help with medical bills while awaiting a verdict or settlement for an injury claim. If you do not have health insurance or are concerned that it will not cover much of your medical costs, you may want to consider purchasing MedPay. Car crash injuries can be very expensive to treat, and many people do not have the financial means to pay for it. Missing payments will likely hurt your credit score and may result in calls from debt collectors, adding more stress to an already stressful situation.

Using Your Health Insurance Policy

If you have health insurance, this may be the best option while you wait for a potential settlement of your claim. This is what often happens, as many drivers do not have MedPay coverage in their car insurance policies. However, the health insurance company is likely to pursue reimbursement from the liable insurance company for any costs they paid out. This process is called subrogation, and it means your compensation award would be reduced by the amount your health insurance paid out. With the help from one of our attorneys, you may be able to negotiate a lower payback amount so you may be able to keep more of the compensation your lawyer recovers.

Negotiate a Payment Agreement with the Medical Provider

If you do not have MedPay or health insurance, our attorneys may be able to work with you to find medical providers who will agree to treat you on a contingency basis. This means that our attorneys would negotiate with the doctor or medical center to have their services paid for after your claim is settled or a verdict is reached in your favor.

Other Options

Every injury victim’s life situation is just as unique as his or her injury claim, which means that some people may have other options to help pay for medical treatment:
  • Medicaid
  • Medicare
  • Veterans Affairs Benefits
Family members or loved ones may also be willing and able to help. You could pay them back after you receive your settlement. Hospitals and other medical providers are often willing to negotiate monthly payment amounts. You may be able to negotiate an amount you can afford to pay until your injury claim is settled. However, it is important to remember if you miss a payment, the provider may demand you immediately pay the rest of the bill. It is important not to delay medical treatment, as it could result in the worsening of your injuries. If you are concerned about how to pay your medical bills, Roden Law may be able to help.

Call Roden Law Today to Discuss Your Claim

Whether you need help filing your injury claim or negotiating a lower rate for your medical bills, our attorneys are prepared to assist you. Do not let the insurance companies take advantage of you. Let the attorneys at Roden Law stand up for your rights. We do not charge you anything while we work on your claim and only get paid if you do.

Epilepsy affects millions worldwide, including about 3.4 million Americans, roughly 2.9 million adults and 456,000 children, according to the CDC. Given the potential for seizures and blackouts, it raises an important question: should people with epilepsy be allowed to drive? Moreover, can they be held liable for car accidents caused by seizures? At Roden Law, our dedicated car accident lawyers in Charleston specialize in handling complex cases involving medical conditions or medication. If you've been involved in a seizure-related accident or experienced a seizure while driving, our knowledgeable attorneys can provide a free case evaluation to explain your rights and assess whether you're eligible for compensation.

Dangers of Driving with Epilepsy/Seizures

Driving with epilepsy can pose significant risks, even if you're currently taking medication to control your symptoms. CDC data from 2015, published in 2018, found that fewer than half (about 42 percent) of U.S. adults taking epilepsy medication had been seizure-free in the previous year. An epileptic incident can occur at any time, and in the moments leading up to it and during a seizure, these are some of the symptoms that could impair your ability to drive safely:
  • Seizure-induced confusion
  • Loss of consciousness
  • Uncontrollable body jerking
  • Cognitive impairment
  • Anxiety
  • Staring spells or feeling “spaced out”
  • Headaches
  • Temporary paralysis after a seizure
  • Memory lapses
  • Temporary loss of bowel control

Driver’s License Requirements for Seizures

In Georgia, a noncommercial license cannot be denied for epilepsy unless a seizure occurred within the previous six months (O.C.G.A. § 40-5-35), and drivers whose seizures occur only during sleep may qualify for a limited license even within that window (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 375-3-5-.02). South Carolina sets no fixed seizure-free period; the SCDMV reviews the license application's 12-month seizure question and decides fitness case by case with advice from its Medical Advisory Board (S.C. Code § 56-1-221). For other states, see the Epilepsy Foundation's state-by-state driving-law summaries.

Reporting Medical Limitations

Neither Georgia nor South Carolina requires doctors to report patients with epilepsy, but Georgia lets physicians report unsafe drivers and shields them from liability (O.C.G.A. § 40-5-35). In Georgia, relatives, courts, judges, law enforcement officers, or citizens can also submit non-anonymous requests for review, and the Department of Driver Services (DDS) may then require a medical evaluation and revoke the license if the driver does not comply. In South Carolina, the SCDMV can order an examination of a driver it has good cause to believe is unfit and suspend, revoke, or restrict the license (S.C. Code § 56-1-270).

Determining Liability for a Crash Involving Seizures

If a person has a seizure and causes an accident, it doesn't automatically make them legally responsible for the collision. Courts in both Georgia and South Carolina ask whether the seizure was foreseeable, weighing the individual's history of epileptic events or seizures, whether they were under the care of a doctor for epilepsy, and whether they were driving inside Georgia's six-month no-seizure window or against a doctor's advice. While a seizure's involvement in the accident may attribute some fault to the person with the medical condition, the issue remains complex, particularly if they had no prior diagnosis or seizure history.

How Comparative Fault Comes into Play

Georgia uses a modified comparative negligence system to apportion fault between two or more parties whose negligence contributed to an accident. According to this system, if you were less than 50 percent at fault for the accident, you can still pursue compensation for the damages you sustained. However, your level of recovery will be reduced by your fault percentage. For example, if you are found 10 percent liable for the accident, you can only receive 90 percent of the total value of your damages. In Georgia, if you are found 50 percent or more at fault, you cannot recover any damages (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). South Carolina reduces damages the same way but bars recovery only at 51 percent (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.), so a driver found exactly half at fault recovers half there and nothing in Georgia.

Call Us Right Now for Help with Your Claim

If you've been injured in an accident caused by someone experiencing a seizure or if you had a seizure while driving, it's essential to seek the help of an attorney experienced in personal injury law. 

The dedicated legal team at Roden Law can review the circumstances surrounding your case and explain your rights to you. We work on a contingency fee basis, so you are charged nothing unless we recover compensation for your accident. Call us today to schedule a confidential and complimentary consultation.

If you were involved in a car accident due to loud music, you may be eligible to pursue compensation. Our Charleston car accident lawyers can walk you through your legal rights during a free consultation.

Call today to learn about your potential legal rights. 1-844-RESULTS.

Risks of Driving With Loud Music

Drivers have a legal duty to stay focused on the road. Loud music can become distracting and disrupt a driver's ability to pay attention, which could lead to following types of distractions:

Cognitive Overload

Drivers may experience cognitive overload when the brain is overwhelmed by too many things happening at once. For instance, loud music with complex lyrics could leave drivers with less mental capacity to process important information. A driver could be too busy singing the lyrics to a song and fail to see a traffic light or stop sign, causing them to fail yield the right of way. This could in a crash if another vehicle is already traveling through the intersection.

Auditory Distraction

Auditory distractions are external sounds that prevent drivers from hearing vital cues on the road or highway. Loud music is an auditory distraction that conceals crucial environmental noise around you as you drive. For instance, it can conceal sirens, horns and tire screeches. If drivers cannot hear emergency vehicles approaching, it could lead to a serious crash involving another driver or emergency vehicle.

Attention Shifts

Loud music can cause drivers to shift their attention between listening to music and paying attention to the road. This shift can result in delayed responses to changes in traffic conditions or obstacles. For instance, if a driver is engaging in their music, they may not realize that they must slow down due to traffic congestions. As a result, drivers may not react swiftly to sudden changes, causing them to rear-end a vehicle in front of them.

The Impact of Loud Music in Charleston

Driving in Charleston is already tricky due to its historic cobblestone streets, busy tourist areas and community events. Loud music can present these driving challenges:

Narrow, Historic Streets

Charleston's historic district is beautiful, but has some narrow streets that limit visibility. Drivers must stay alert for other cars, pedestrians and cyclists. Loud music can muffle sirens and horns that distract drivers, making it harder to notice the signs of potential hazards and increasing accident risks.

Heavy Tourist Traffic

Tourist traffic in Charleston can create unpredictable driving conditions. Visitors may not be familiar with local road rules or the flow of traffic, particularly if they end up on one of the many one-way streets. Loud music can distract drivers from adapting to these unpredictable patterns, making it harder to navigate safely through busy downtown areas.

Pedestrian-Friendly Zones

Charleston is known for its vibrant pedestrian zones, including Broad Street and Rainbow Row. Pedestrian-heavy areas require extra vigilance. Drivers playing loud music might not notice pedestrians crossing streets or walking near the road, increasing the risk of pedestrian accidents.

How to Reduce Car Crash Related to Loud Music

Understanding the risks of loud music is the first step toward safer driving. Here are practical strategies to mitigate these risks:

Keep Volume at a Safe Level

One of the simplest ways to reduce the risks associated with loud music is to keep the volume at a moderate level. Ensure that the music does not overpower important sounds from the environment. The general recommendation is to keep the volume low enough so that you can hear sirens and other critical auditory cues.

Choose Music Wisely

The type of music you listen to can have an impact on your driving. Fast paced or highly energetic music can be more distracting than soothing or instrumental music. Opt for music that is calming and less likely to cause cognitive overload. Instrumental tracks or music with fewer lyrics may be less distracting and help you to maintain focus.

Avoid Distractions While Driving

Adjusting the music or making changes to the audio system while driving can be distracting. Minimize these interactions by setting up your playlist or radio stations before you start driving. If you need to adjust your any settings, pull over safely before doing so.

Be Mindful of Your Well-Being

Your own state of mind and physical condition play a role in how music affects your driving. If you are feeling tired or stressed, loud music can exacerbate these feelings and impair your driving further. Ensure that you are well-rested and in a good mental state before getting behind the wheel.

How Claims May Be Affected in Loud Music Related Car Crashes?

Every case is different. However, if loud music contributes to an accident, it can be a factor in determining liability. In car accident cases, distractions like loud music may be considered when assessing fault. A car accident due to someone being distracted, could mean they are at-fault for the car crash. Since South Carolina is an at-fault state, the driver liable for the crash is responsible for covering your medical expenses and other damages. However, you need to speak to an attorney to know your specific legal options.

Contact Roden Law Today

After a car crash, call our firm to discuss your potential case further. Our lawyers at Roden Law want to help you get the compensation you deserve. We can answer your legal questions during a free consultation. There are no upfront cost or fees to speak to our attorney about the details of your scenario.

To learn more call: 1-844-RESULTS.

Who Is At-Fault for Backing-Up Crashes in Charleston?

Most of the time, the party backing up is going to be liable. That said, even backing-up crashes in South Carolina can be complex. Liability is not always clear or straightforward, and sometimes fault may be shared. Here are some of the parties who could be liable for a South Carolina backing-up crash:
  • The driver backing-up or out: Often the primary at-fault party since it is their duty to make sure the path is clear before backing out
  • A driver in the feeder lane: May share fault if they were speeding by to avoid having to wait or were not paying attention
  • The vehicle owner: Might share some fault if they knowingly allowed an incompetent driver to use their car
  • An employer: Could be held liable if the backing-up driver was operating a company vehicle on company time
  • Vehicle manufacturer: May be at fault if a vehicle defect, such as a sudden unintended acceleration (SUA), led to the crash
  • Government entity or property manager: Potentially liable if poor road design or negligent maintenance played a role in causing the incident.

What If I Am Partially to Blame for a Backing-Up Crash in Charleston?

It is not uncommon for two parties to share liability for a backing-up crash. South Carolina follows a modified comparative negligence rule, so you may still be able to recover at least a portion of your damages. The percentage of fault you are assessed with gets deducted from any awarded compensation. You cannot, however, recover compensation if you are more than 50 percent liable. Even if you are 51 percent at fault, you are barred from recovering damages. Right after a crash, it is important that you do not try to determine whether you were at fault. Be honest about what you believe happened, but let crash investigators do their job and figure out other factors that may have led to the crash. We recommend you consider consulting with an experienced auto accident lawyer. Having a lawyer represent you means that someone is fighting to protect your rights and legal interests. This includes disputing any liability unfairly assessed against you.

How Backing-Up Crashes Happen

Backing-up crashes are pretty common, no matter where you live. They are often the result of errors or negligence, such as driver distractions or trusting a backing-up camera too much. These accidents can happen in various settings and circumstances, potentially leading to serious injuries and property damage. Being mindful of how and where backing-up crashes occur is important. It is also an important reminder of how drivers and pedestrians need to take preventive measures to avoid causing harm to someone in a backing-up accident.

Where Do Backing Crashes Happen?

Backing-up crashes are most likely to occur when people are backing out of a parking space or driveway. It is important to stay alert when backing up or when approaching someone who is backing up. It is a driver's duty to stay focused on the road and what is happening around their vehicle at all times. Typically, backing up crashes happen in these areas:
  • Parking lots: Drivers backing out of parking spaces collide with passing vehicles or pedestrians.
  • Driveways: Motorists backing out onto the street fail to see oncoming traffic.
  • Residential areas: Drivers reversing without noticing children, pets or obstacles behind their vehicle.
  • Construction sites: Workers or equipment operators backing up heavy machinery without proper spotters.
  • Loading docks: Truck drivers failing to check blind spots or misjudging distances while reversing to load or unload cargo.
  • Busy streets: Drivers attempting to back into parallel parking spaces in high-traffic areas.
  • Intersections: Motorists backing up after missing a turn or entering the wrong lane.
  • Highways: Drivers reversing on shoulders or emergency lanes after missing an exit.

What Should I Do After a Backing-Up Crash?

If you are involved in a backing-up crash, it is important to remain calm. Any kind of accident can shake you up a bit, even if it seems minor.

Report the Incident

Be sure to report the accident to the proper authorities, even if it seems no one is hurt. This documentation will be important if you later find you have medical costs or vehicle damage and need to file a claim.

Gather Information

Gather information from other involved parties, of course, and check for witnesses who may have seen what happened.

Call for Help

Call 9-1-1 if anyone is injured to get medical assistance to the scene as soon as possible.

Get Medical Attention

Even if you do not think you are hurt, getting examined at the ER is a good idea. You could have internal injuries and can only find that out if you get diagnostic imaging done. Your medical records, which document the date and details of your ER visit, also help link your injuries to the crash that caused them. This is vital to any legal claim you may later pursue.

Seek Legal Help

Seek legal help as soon after the crash as possible to determine if you may have a claim.

Call our law office to speak with a member of our legal team about your situation. Your initial consultation is completely free, and there are no upfront costs or fees if we represent you.

Dangerous Rural Highways in the Charleston Area

Charleston's rural areas have several dangerous routes where drivers need to be especially alert and take precautionary measures. These hazardous major rural routes include:
  • Highway 17 North: This highway runs through the towns of Awendaw and McClellanville. This remote route is known for its high traffic volume and wildlife crossings, which increases the risk of a crash.
  • Highway 61:This remote highway, also known as Ashley River Road, considered hazardous due to its narrow lanes and lack of shoulders.
  • Highway 41:  Another well-known rural highway that runs through Francis Marion National Forest. It dangerous to drivers, especially in low light and adverse weather conditions, due to limited lighting and sharp curves.
  • Highway 45: Drivers may be involved in a car accident on this highway due to its higher speeds, lack of safety features and limited emergency services.

Why Are Rural Roads So Dangerous?

Rural roads near Charleston present unique challenges that many drivers underestimate, such as:

Limited Emergency Response Available to Due Being Remote

After an accident, help takes longer to arrive in some rural areas. This can create critical and devastating circumstances for crash victims who are severely injured. For example, if someone suffers severe burns or lacerations, getting emergency medical care could make the difference in how well the victims recover.

Poor Road Maintenance

Rural roads are often maintained less frequently than city streets. Potholes, crumbling shoulders and faded lane markings add to already treacherous driving conditions. Poorly maintained roads during adverse weather make it even more challenging for drivers to see at night. For example, uneven lanes may cause side-swipe car crashes. Potholes in bad condition could cause a vehicle’s tire to blow out, making a driver lose control of their car.

Lack of Safety Features

Unlike urban roads, many rural routes lack the following safety features. These safety features are designed to help drivers avoid accidents and view hidden hazards.
  • Guardrails
  • Reflective markers
  • Adequate shoulder space
  • Streetlights
  • Clear signage

Environmental Factors

Common natural hazards in Charleston’s rural area include:
  • Flooding During Heavy Rain: If there is flooding in a particular area, vehicles may get stuck. Depending on how high the water rises, some drivers could drown in their vehicles.
  • Wildlife Crossings: Deer or wild boars could suddenly dart into the road. If drivers are unable to see them, it could cause a collision.
  • Fallen Trees and Branches: In rural areas, maintaining the roads can be difficult due to the exclusivity of the area. Speeding drivers risk crashing into large, fallen trees or branches.
  • Standing Water After Storms: Depending on the road, standing water could form after a storm, causing some vehicles to get stuck in mud. Standing water may also cause drivers to swerve, leading to a hydroplane crash.

Driver Behavior

Some drivers may be more reckless on rural roads, but these habits could lead to a car crash.
  • Higher speeds due to less traffic
  • Increased distracted driving
  • Overconfidence on familiar roads
  • Impaired driving due to fewer ride-share options

Are Fatal Car Accidents More Likely To Happen on Rural Roads?

According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, rural accidents account for about 43 percent of all traffic fatalities from 2017 to 2021. These are the types of accidents that are likely to be fatal when driving in rural areas:
  • Head-On Collisions: If there are not enough traffic signs or lane markings, drivers may maneuver into the wrong lane, causing head-on collisions.
  • Single-Vehicle Accidents: Vehicles could be involved in a single-vehicle crash if the roads have sharp curves or lack guardrails.
  • Night-time Crashes: Night-time crashes are likely to happen if there are not enough streetlights, which could make it difficult to see other drivers.
  • Rollover Crashes: Rollover crashes are more likely to occur in rural areas when vehicles try to take sharp turns too quickly. SUVs, vans and  trucks, which have a higher center of gravity, are especially likely to flip over in this situation.

What Can Drivers Do To Prevent Car Crashes?

Drivers can significantly reduce their risk of crashing along a rural highway by following several key safety practices.

Slow Down

Reduce your speed and maintain extra following distance, especially at night or during bad weather.

Drive Defensively

Be prepare for unexpected curves and wildlife crossings. Keep your headlights on at night, especially if there are not enough streetlights.

Avoid Distractions

Avoid distractions like cell phones. Rural roads have fewer safety features and require more focused attention. In these areas, you could encounter farm equipment, wildlife or stopped school buses around blind curves.

Maintain Your Vehicle

Regular vehicle maintenance is crucial. Before traveling on rural routes, ensure your tires, brakes and lights are in good condition.

Watch Out for Shoulder Drop-Offs

Watch for shoulder drop-offs and avoid sudden steering corrections if your wheels drift off the pavement. Instead, slowly ease off the accelerator and gradually return to the road.

Keep Essential Items in Your Car

If you often drive in rural areas, having these items in your car could be helpful, as you may not have access to roadside assistance or emergency responders.
  • First aid kit
  • Flashlight
  • Reflective triangles or flares
  • Fire extinguishers
  • Spare tire, jack and lug wrench
  • Jumper cables
  • And more

What Permanent Injuries May Result From a Car Accident?

A permanent injury is one that does not heal completely, or a condition that will continue to affect you for the rest of your life. These types of injuries often lead to chronic pain, loss of function and in some cases, permanent disability. Some common examples of permanent injuries sustained in car accidents include:
  • Traumatic brain injuries affecting cognitive function
  • Spinal cord damage leading to paralysis
  • Severe burns causing disfigurement
  • Loss of limbs requiring prosthetics
  • Joint injuries resulting in chronic pain
  • Vision or hearing loss
  • Nerve damage causing persistent numbness
The impact of these injuries extends beyond just physical pain. Many people with permanent injuries face challenges related to employment, personal relationships and daily activities. Some may need lifelong medical care, assistive devices or ongoing therapy.

How Do I Calculate the Value of My Charleston Car Accident Claim?

While every car accident case is different, permanent injury settlements could range from hundreds of thousands or more. Factors impacting the overall value of your claim include:

Extent and Severity of Your Injuries

The more severe and permanent the injury, the higher the potential value of your claim. For example, an amputation or paralysis will typically result in a much larger settlement compared to a broken bone that heals within a few months. If your injuries cause permanent disability, requiring ongoing care or preventing you from working, the value of your claim will reflect these long-term consequences.

Medical Expenses

The cost of medical treatment after a car crash plays a significant role when determining the value of your claim. For permanent injuries, treatment costs can add up quickly and may include:
  • Emergency care immediately following the accident
  • Diagnostic testing
  • Surgery or other major medical procedures
  • Long-term physical therapy
  • Assistive devices (e.g., wheelchairs, prosthetics)
  • Pain management
  • Home healthcare services
  • Rehabilitation therapy
  • Pain and suffering
In South Carolina, victims can recover compensation for past, present and future medical expenses. If your injuries require lifelong medical treatment, this can significantly increase the value of your claim.

Lost Wages and Loss of Earning Capacity

If your permanent injuries prevent you from working or significantly limit the type of work you can perform, you are entitled to compensation for lost wages. This includes both the wages you have already lost and the wages you will lose in the future. The longer the impact of your injury on your ability to earn a living, the more compensation you may be able to claim for loss of earning capacity. If your injury limits your ability to work in the same field or results in a permanent reduction in income, the value of your claim will reflect this financial loss.

Pain and Suffering

Pain and suffering is a non-economic damage that compensates you for the physical pain, emotional distress and reduced quality of life caused by your injuries. Unlike medical expenses, pain and suffering damages do not have an exact formula. However, the more severe and permanent the injury, the higher the potential compensation. Some of the pain and suffering factors that may influence the value of your claim include:
  • The intensity and duration of pain
  • Whether you will experience ongoing pain for the rest of your life
  • The emotional toll of living with a permanent disability
  • The impact the injury has on your mental health (depression, anxiety, PTSD)
  • The way your injury affects your ability to participate in normal activities or enjoy life

Impact on Daily Life and Relationships

Permanent injuries often lead to changes in a person’s daily life, including a reduced ability to perform everyday tasks, like driving, cooking or caring for children. The ability to engage in social, recreational or family activities may be severely impacted. The more your injury alters your ability to live a normal, fulfilling life, the greater the value of your claim. Additionally, how your injury affects your relationships with your spouse, children or other close family members should be factored into your compensation.

Insurance Coverage and Liability

The amount of insurance coverage the at-fault driver carries affects the value of your claim as well. South Carolina law requires drivers to carry a minimum of $25,000 in liability insurance per person and $50,000 per accident for bodily injury. However, if the at-fault driver is underinsured or uninsured, this can complicate the claims process. If you have uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage, your own insurance policy may come into play. What Permanent Injuries May Result From a Car Accident?

Extent and Severity of Your Injuries

How Can Prescription Medication Affect My Driving?

Effects from prescription medication can cause drivers to swerve in and out of lanes or loose control of their vehicle. Even medications prescribed by trusted healthcare professionals can create dangerous driving conditions if not carefully managed. Prescription medications can significantly impair driving performance by:
  • Causing drowsiness or sedation
  • Reducing reaction times
  • Blurring vision
  • Causing dizziness
  • Impairing cognitive function
  • Decreasing motor coordination

What Types of Prescription Medication Could Lead to a Car Accident?

Several categories of prescription medications can compromise driving safety, such as:
  • Opioids: Used for managing pain and can cause drowsiness, slowed reaction times and impaired coordination.
  • Benzodiazepines: Medications like Xanax and Valium could be prescribed for anxiety and insomnia, which can lead to drowsiness, dizziness and poor judgment.
  • Antidepressants: Antidepressants like Prozac and Zoloft are used to treat depression but can lead to dizziness or blurred vision.
  • Antihistamines: This medication is used for allergies and cold symptoms. Drugs like Benadryl can cause drowsiness and reduced concentration.
  • Sleep Medications: Medication for individuals who have trouble sleeping can cause drivers to feel drowsy. For example, Ambien is a common sleep medication that is known for increasing the risk of accidents.

What Symptoms Could Lead to an Accident After Taking Prescription Medication?

Recognizing potential driving risks involves understanding specific symptoms:
  • Excessive yawning or feeling extremely tired
  • Difficulty maintaining lane position
  • Delayed reaction to traffic signals or sudden movements
  • Feeling disconnected or "foggy"
  • Feeling unusually relaxed or disoriented

Is It Illegal To Drive After Taking Prescription Medication?

In South Carolina, driving under the influence (DUI) laws still apply to prescription medications if they impair your ability to drive safely. While having a valid prescription is legal, driving while impaired is not. Under Section 56-5-2930, this law states that it is illegal to drive a vehicle under the influence of any substance, including prescription medication, if it impairs your ability to drive safely. Even with a valid prescription, you can be legally responsible if your medication causes a car accident. Law enforcement can still charge you with:
  • Driving under the influence
  • Reckless driving
  • Negligent operation of a vehicle

What Should I Do if I'm Injured Due to a Driver Being on Prescribed Medication?

Proving medication-related impairment requires thorough investigation and gathering evidence. If you have been injured in a car crash because another driver was impaired from prescribe medication, it is highly recommended to seek medical attention and reach out to a licensed car accident attorney. They can help you with filing a claim and navigating the complex legal process. If you have been involved in an accident potentially caused by prescription medication, take these steps:
  • Document everything at the accident scene
  • Get diagnostic tests for your injuries
  • Collect contact information from witnesses
  • Request a copy of the police report
  • Keep all medical records

How Can Drivers Prevent Driving Under the Influence of Prescription Medication?

Before drivers operate a vehicle, it is important that they know the preventative measures that they need to take to avoid any road hazards. Some steps that can be taken to prevent impaired driving due to prescription medications are:

Understanding Your Medication

Always read the label and warnings on your prescription medications. Look for any indications that the medication may cause drowsiness, dizziness or impair your ability to drive.

Consult Your Doctor

Ask your healthcare if your medication might affect your driving. They can provide you with guidance on when to take your medication and whether it is safe to drive while under certain medications.

Monitor Your Reaction

Everyone’s body react differently to medication. Pay attention to how you feel after taking your medication. If you experience any symptoms such as drowsiness or blurred vision, avoid driving.

Avoid Mixing Medication

Be cautious about taking multiple medications at once. Sometimes the combination of multiple medications could increase the risk of impairment. Also, avoid mixing medication with alcohol as it can cause you to become impaired before you drive.

Plan Ahead

If you know that you have to take medication that could impair your ability to drive, take alternative transportation like Uber, a public transit or ask a friend or family member for a ride.

Stay Informed

Stay up to date with any new information about your medications and their potential side effects. Your pharmacist can provide you with resourceful information.

Why Am I So Tired After My Charleston Car Crash?

After a car crash, your body undergoes physical and emotional stress, which can lead to extreme fatigue. Injuries, even those that seem minor, can drain your energy as your body works to heal. Adrenaline and shock from the accident can mask pain initially, but once those effects wear off, exhaustion can set in. Additionally, anxiety, sleep disturbances and the stress from dealing with accident-related matters can contribute to feeling overly tired. Fatigue can also be linked to internal injuries that might not be immediately apparent, such as whiplash, concussions or soft tissue damage. These injuries can disrupt your normal sleep patterns and cause lingering pain, both of which are major contributors to post-accident exhaustion.

When Should I See a Doctor About Car Crash Fatigue?

You should see a doctor if your fatigue after a car crash lasts longer than a few days or if it is affecting your ability to function normally. Here are some signs that indicate it is time to seek medical attention:
  • Fatigue lasts more than a few days
  • You have trouble working or completing daily tasks
  • You experience headaches, dizziness or memory problems
  • Sleep disturbances or trouble resting
  • Fatigue worsens or does not improve over time
  • You notice new or increasing pain alongside fatigue

What Injuries Could Make Me Feel Unusually Tired?

Identifying these hidden injuries can help explain your exhaustion and guide you toward the right treatment.

Whiplash and Soft Tissue Injuries

Whiplash and other soft tissue injuries can cause pain and stiffness, leading to exhaustion as your body works to heal. Some other symptoms of whiplash and soft tissue injuries may include limited motion in the neck area and headaches.

Do I Have the Right To Refuse Certain Medical Treatment?

Yes, you absolutely have the legal right to refuse medical treatment after a car accident. This right is protected under both state and federal law, stemming from the fundamental principle of bodily autonomy. However, understanding the consequences of this decision is essential. Medical professionals recommend treatment to ensure your well-being and document any injuries diagnosed as a result of a car accident. Even if you do not think you have any injuries seek medical attention. Some injuries may not be apparent right away. Injuries like whiplash or internal bleeding can have delayed symptoms that worsen over time. When you refuse medical treatment, you might be putting both your health and your legal right at risk.

How Can Refusing Medical Treatment Impact My Claim?

The decision to refuse medical treatment can have profound consequences for your car accident claim. Insurance companies and defense attorneys will scrutinize every aspect of your case, including your medical decisions.

Weakens Your Injury Claim Evidence

Medical documentation serves as crucial evidence in personal injury cases. When you seek immediate medical attention, healthcare providers create detailed records that gives insight into your injuries, treatment plans and prognosis. These records establish a clear link between the accident and your injuries, strengthening your claim. Without this documentation, proving the extent and cause of your injuries becomes significantly more challenging.

No Evidence for Pain and Suffering

Medical records provide objective evidence of your pain and suffering. For example, they can give insight into why you have chronic pain and how difficult your physical therapy appointments are. When you refuse treatment, you lose the opportunity to have professional documentation of your condition immediately after the accident, which can be difficult to reconstruct later.

Gives Insurers Reason To Deny Payment

Insurance companies are always looking for reasons to minimize or deny claims. Refusing medical treatment gives them powerful ammunition to argue that your injuries were not serious or were not caused by the accident. They might insist that if you were truly injured, you would have sought immediate medical attention. Insurance adjusters may also argue that your injuries worsened because you did not seek prompt medical care, making you partially responsible for your current condition. Their assumptions could lead to claims denial.

Decrease the Value of Your Claim

When calculating the value of your claim, insurance companies and courts look at various factors, including the promptness and consistency of your medical treatment. Refusing treatment can significantly decrease your claim's value because:
  • The gap between the accident and your eventual treatment makes it harder to prove causation
  • Your injuries may have worsened, but the insurer can argue this was due to your negligence in seeking treatment
  • The lack of immediate medical documentation makes it difficult to establish the initial severity of your injuries

What Evidence Should I Gather if I Refuse Medical Treatment After a Car Crash?

If you refuse medical treatment after a car crash, it can be more challenging to prove your injuries and claim compensation. However, you can still gather other evidence to support your case, such as:
  • Police Report: This document provides an official account of the incident and can help establish fault.
  • Photographs and Videos: Visual evidence can help demonstrate the severity of the crash.
  • Witness Statements: Witnesses account of what happened at the car crash scene can align with your version of events, which can help strengthen your case.
  • Receipts and Bills: Save all your receipts related to expenses incurred due to the accident, like vehicle repairs, transportation costs, and any over-the-counter medications or treatment you purchased.
  • Employment Records: Document any time missed from work and any impact on your ability to perform your job. This could show the financial impact the accident had on your injuries.

Reasons Car Crash Victims Refuse Treatment

Car crash victims may refuse medical treatment for several reasons. Sometimes victims may refuse treatment if they have a suspicion or a concern that they think may hinder them. Common reasons include:
  • Fear of missing work or losing income
  • Anxiety about medical procedures or hospitals
  • Belief that injuries are minor and will heal on their own
  • Religious or personal beliefs about certain medical treatments
  • Financial concerns about medical bills and lack of insurance coverage
While these concerns are valid, it is important to remember that delaying or refusing medical treatment can cost you more in the long run, both in terms of your health and your legal claim. Most personal injury attorneys can help you find medical providers who will treat you on a lien basis, meaning they will wait for payment until your case settles.

What Is the Most Common Shoulder Injury From a Car Accident?

Car accidents frequently cause various shoulder injuries, with rotator cuff tears being the most common. The rotator cuff consists of four muscles and tendons that stabilize your shoulder joint and enable arm movement. During a collision, the sudden impact can cause these tissues to stretch, tear or become severely damaged. While rotator cuff injuries are one of the most frequent injuries, other common shoulder injuries from car accidents include:
  • Shoulder Fractures: Breaks in the bones of the shoulder can cause victims to experience severe pain, swelling and difficulty moving the arm.
  • Shoulder Dislocation: This occurs when the upper arm bone pops out of the shoulder socket, causing intense pain and limited mobility.
  • Labral Tears: The labrum is a ring of cartilage that surrounds the shoulder socket and helps keep the joint stable. Tears in this cartilage can lead to pain and instability in the shoulder.
  • Bursitis: This involves inflammation of small, fluid-filled sacs that cushion your joints and reduce friction between bones, tendons and muscles. This may lead to pain and swelling, particularly during arm movement.
  • AC Joint Separation: This may happen when the joint connecting your collarbone to shoulder blade becomes damaged due to a fall or direct blow to the shoulder, leading to a visible bump on the shoulder.
Shoulder injuries occur when the body is thrown forward during impact, especially if you are gripping the steering wheel tightly. Side-impact collisions can also cause direct trauma to the shoulder area.

How Do I Know if My Shoulder Injuries Are Severe?

Recognizing the severity of a shoulder injury early can ensure you receive proper treatment and detailed documentation for your injury claim. Warning signs of a serious shoulder injury include:
  • Visible deformity or swelling
  • Weakness in the arm or shoulder
  • Bruising around the shoulder area
  • Inability to raise your arm above your head
  • Inability to raise your arm above your head
  • Pain that worsens at night or prevents sleep
  • Numbness or tingling extending down your arm
  • A popping or grinding sensation when moving your shoulder
Do not dismiss these symptoms as minor or temporary. Some shoulder injuries may seem manageable initially but can become worse without proper medical attention. Additionally, adrenaline released during the accident can mask pain, making injuries appear less severe than they are.

What Evidence Can Link My Shoulder Injury to the Car Accident?

Building a strong connection between your shoulder injury and the car accident requires solid evidence. Below are the types of evidence that can help link your injuries to the accident.

Medical Documentation

If you go to the emergency room or urgent care, be sure that you obtain records that shows details of your injuries. Documents show immediate care after a car accident, prove the severity of your injuries and could indicate the type of medical treatment you will need to recover. Other medical documentations you may use as evidence may include:
  • Physical therapy records
  • Treatment plans and physician notes
  • Documentation of any surgical procedures
  • Diagnostic imaging results (X-rays, MRI, CT scans)

Accident-Related Evidence

A police report detailing the crash circumstances can help indicate who was at fault. Photographs of the accident scene may show the point of impact and how the crash occurred. If you could not take photos at the scene, check for video footage from nearby surveillance cameras or dashcams, including your own or another driver’s. If any witnesses observe the accident, they can provide statements describing the collision. This evidence strengthen your case, especially when witnesses account of what happened aligns with your perspective of how the accident happened. After you take your vehicle to the repair shop, be sure to get a repair estimate so that it may be added into your compensation. It is a good idea to have any evidence that shows damages to your property so that you may receive compensation for it.

Expert Testimony

Testimony from medical experts and accident reconstruction specialists can provide valuable insight into the car crash. A medical professional can explain the extent and severity of your injuries. When the cause of a crash is not clear, we may consult with an accident reconstruction specialist. These specially trained professionals examine the same evidence, but they use scientific methods combined with high tech tools to recreate the crash. These crash scene recreations often clarify complex crashes and help to establish who is at-fault. Some car crash victims may have challenges with going back to work after a collision. As a result, they can miss work or may have a reduced earning capacity if they can not return to the same type of work they were used to doing before the car accident. An occupational professional can describe how your injury affects your ability to work so that you may receive compensation for lost wages, future earning potential and diminished capacity to perform your job. Their testimony can ensure you have a solid case and help ensure you receive fair compensation for the financial impact of your injuries.

How Much Compensation Can I Receive for My Shoulder Injuries?

Every case is different; therefore, the compensation amount may vary depending on the severity of the injury, duration it takes to recover and how the crash impact on your daily activities. It is recommended to speak to a licensed attorney to get a better understanding of your injuries. They can determine your case value based on the specific, unique details and events of your case. Below are the type of compensation you may be eligible for after sustaining a shoulder injury in a car crash.

Economic Damages

Economic damages are the types of compensation that is related to monetary value. Examples of economic damages include:
  • Lost wages during recovery
  • Current and future medical expenses
  • Physical therapy and rehabilitation costs
  • Transportation expenses for medical appointments
  • Reduced earning capacity if the injury affects your ability to work

Non-Economic Damages

Non-economic damages focus on compensating car crash victims for the intangible losses that resulted from an injury. Some of these non-economic damages are:
  • Pain and suffering
  • Emotional distress
  • Loss of enjoyment of life
  • Impact on personal relationships
  • Physical impairment or disfigurement

What Should You Tell Your Health Provider About Your Injuries?

Explain How the Injury Happened

Provide a clear account of the accident and how your injuries occurred. You should not share unrelated details, like who caused the crash or how fast you were going. However, including details about the direction of impact, the type of car you were driving and your position in the vehicle gives your doctor more insight into the injuries you may have sustained. Inform your doctor, for instance, if you were wearing a seat belt and describe any immediate symptoms you experienced. The type of crash, such as a rear end, side impact or head on collision, can also help your doctor better understand the pain or injuries you may be experiencing.

Previous Injuries

Inform your doctor about any pre-existing conditions or previous injuries, particularly those involving the same areas affected in your recent accident. This transparency helps your healthcare provider distinguish new injuries from existing conditions. For instance, if you had a prior knee condition, your doctor could assess how the accident may have exacerbated it. Documenting the specific impact of the accident can also provide your doctor with valuable insights into your medical history. When your doctor has a complete understanding of your medical background, they can develop a tailored and effective treatment plan to address your needs.

All Your Symptoms

Report every symptom you experience, even those that seem minor or unrelated. Seemingly minor symptoms may indicate more serious underlying injuries. What Is a Traumatic Brain Injury?

A Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) occurs when a sudden trauma causes damage to the brain. This damage can result from the head violently hitting an object, an object piercing the skull and entering brain tissue or forces that cause the brain to move within the skull, such as violent shaking or blast waves.

How Do Car Crashes Cause Serious Brain Injuries?

Car crashes can cause severe brain injuries through several types of incidents that happen during a car crash. Some incidents may include:
  • Direct Impact Trauma: When the head strikes objects like the steering wheel, windshield, or side window, the force can fracture the skull and damage brain tissue directly.
  • Acceleration-Deceleration Forces: Even without direct head impact, rapid acceleration and deceleration causes the brain to collide with the inner skull wall. This creates bruising (contusions) and tearing of nerve fibers (diffuse axonal injury).
  • Penetrating Injuries: Broken glass, metal fragments or other debris can pierce the skull and enter brain tissue.

Car Crashes Factors Affecting Severity of Injuries

The severity of injuries depends on factors like the vehicle speed at impact and the direction of the collision. If a car crash victim did not wear a seat belt, it could increase the severity of their injuries. In some cases, passengers sitting in the front of the vehicle are more likely to suffer from more serious injuries. Older cars with fewer safety features than newer cars could have higher impacts, which may result in more severe injuries.

Secondary Injuries Worsening Health Conditions

Secondary injuries often develop after the initial trauma due to brain swelling or internal bleeding. These injuries frequently affect vital brain regions that control movement, cognition, speech and other vital functions. Prompt medical treatment is essential to prevent worsening damage and improve recovery outcomes.

What Types of Traumatic Brain Injuries Are Common in Car Crashes?

The violent forces involved in collisions can damage the brain in various ways, from mild concussions to severe trauma requiring intensive medical intervention. Victims should know the different types of brain injuries that can happen in a car crash to help with their recovery, a potential legal case and to navigate through life-altering conditions.

Concussions

A concussion is a type of traumatic brain injury that is caused when your brain collides with the inside of your skull. During a car crash, the sudden stop or impact forces cause your brain to bounce or twist inside the skull. Some of the key symptoms of a concussion:
  • Headaches
  • Confusion
  • Memory problems
  • Vision changes
  • Balance issues
  • Nausea
  • Sensitivity to light/noise
  • Sleep disturbances

Hematomas and Hemorrhages

A violent car crash can tear blood vessels in your brain, leading to two types of life-threatening conditions. One is a hematoma, which occurs when blood collects between your brain and skull, creating dangerous pressure on delicate brain tissue. These blood pools may develop slowly over hours or days after the accident, making them particularly dangerous. Brain hemorrhages present a greater threat, as active bleeding within the brain tissue itself can cause rapid deterioration. The bleeding damages surrounding brain cells and creates swelling that can lead to permanent injury or death without immediate treatment. After any head impact, watch out for severe headaches that intensify, growing confusion, slurred speech and seizures.

Brain Contusions

A brain contusion is bruising of brain tissue that occurs when the force of a crash causes your brain to hit your skull. Like bruises elsewhere on your body, these injuries involve bleeding and swelling inside your brain, which can be life-threatening. Some car crash victims may experience confusion and coordination problems.

Skull Fracture

A skull fracture may occur if a violent car crash impact causes you to crack or shatter your skull. These breaks range from hairline cracks to deep fractures that expose brain tissue.

Coup-Contrecoup Injury

A coup-contrecoup injury is a serious type of traumatic brain injury (TBI) that involves damage at two sites in the brain. The coup is at the site of direct impact, while the opposite side of the brain is known as contrecoup. Symptoms vary depending on which areas of the brain are affected, but may include loss of consciousness, memory problems, nausea and vomiting.

Diffuse Axonal Injury

Car crash victims may sustain diffuse axonal injuries after sudden movement stretches and tears axons, nerve fibers, throughout the brain’s white matter.

Why Do Insurance Companies Fight Brain Injury Claims?

Insurance companies often challenge brain injury claims using tactics to help minimize payouts and protect company profits. Their goals do not align with yours, so they make low initial settlement offers to protect their interests. Other tactics they may try include delaying claim processing or extensively perusing victims' medical histories and social media in an attempt to find contradicting evidence. They frequently dispute causation, arguing symptoms existed before the accident or stem from other conditions. They may even question the severity of your brain injury, especially with mild TBIs where damage may not be visible on standard imaging tests. Insurance companies know brain injury claims can be expensive, potentially involving lifetime care costs, lost wages and reduced earning capacity. They also recognize that proving non-obvious symptoms like cognitive difficulties or personality changes can be challenging for victims. Therefore, it is vital to have solid evidence that links your injuries to the car accident.

What Medical Evidence Can Help to Support My Brain Injury Claim?

Strong medical evidence for brain injury claims includes:
  • Medical Records: Documents from the emergency room and hospital visits, treating physician notes, assessments and neurologist evaluations.
  • Diagnostic Tests: CT, MRI and PET scans can detect what type of TBI car crash victims have, along with EEGs.
  • Specialist Documentation: If car crash victims visit a specialist for their injuries, they can provide neuropsychological evaluations, cognitive function test results and speech or occupational therapy assessments.
  • Supporting Evidence: This type of evidence may include photos of visible injuries, witness statements about behavioral changes and work or school performance records showing decline.

Reasons Drivers Act Recklessly

Drivers engage in reckless behavior for psychological and situational reasons. Emotional states like rage, frustration or aggression often trigger dangerous driving choices. Some drivers feel invincible behind the wheel, causing them to speed, tailgate or weave through traffic without considering the consequences. Young or inexperienced drivers may lack proper risk assessment skills or feel peer pressure to drive dangerously. Some drivers disregard traffic laws, viewing them as inconvenient rather than essential safety measures. This combination of personal, emotional and situational factors creates dangerous conditions on heavily trafficked Charleston roads like I-26. Time pressure plays a significant role. Some drivers may be running late, causing them to rush to work or appointments, resulting in unnecessary risks. Other interruptions can lead to reckless drivers. Distraction from phones, passengers or other activities diverts attention from safe driving practices. Substances like alcohol and drugs can severely impair judgment and reaction time. If drivers take prescription drugs before they drive, it can also alter their behavior and become the root cause of their reckless driving.

What Are the Most Common Forms of Reckless Driving?

Reckless drivers have various types of behaviors and activities that they do. Some of the most common forms of reckless driving are:
  • Distracted Driving: This includes activities like texting, eating, adjusting your seat or review mirror while driving.
  • Speeding: Driving above the speed limit reduces reaction time and increases the risk of accidents.
  • Aggressive Driving: This involves tailgating, weaving through traffic or not yielding to other vehicles
  • Street Racing: Racing on public roads is hazardous and illegal
  • Disregarding Traffic Signs and Laws: Running red lights or not stopping at stop signs

How Does Reckless Driving Lead to an Accident?

Reckless driving creates dangerous situations that quickly escalate into crashes. Excessive speed reduces reaction time and increases impact force. When drivers weave through traffic or tailgate, they leave no safety margin for sudden stops or emergencies. Weather conditions and the flow of traffic could amplify these risks. During coastal storms or heavy tourism seasons, reckless driving becomes especially dangerous on routes like Highway 17 and the Ravenel Bridge. Roads already crowded with commuters, tourists and port traffic become hazardous when reckless drivers ignore safety protocols. In some incidents, reckless drivers can cause multiple-vehicle car accidents. Erratically changing lanes or running a red light can cause multiple vehicle accidents. These chain-reaction accidents frequently cause severe injuries and extensive property damage.

Are Reckless Drivers Always Liable for An Accident?
